freshly cut juice. Olympias of Thebes added hyssop and <term>nitrum</term> <gloss>native sodium carbonate</gloss>. The ash of a stag’s horn taken as a drink. Likewise for a troubled womb. Also, application of bull’s gall with opium, two obols in quantity. It is beneficial to fumigate the womb with deer hair. They relate that when hinds feel they are pregnant, they swallow a small stone, which is found in their excrement, or in the womb (for it is also found there), and if kept and tied on, it aids labor. Small bones are also found in the heart and womb that are very useful for pregnant women and those in labor. For concerning the pumice stone that is found in the uterus of cows in a similar way, we spoke in the nature of cattle. Wolf’s fat, when applied, softens the womb. It also avails against harmful applications for their pains. And it is not useless. Or if it is for those beginning to labor, it should be near what she eats. To such a degree that it even avails against harmful applications. And truly, it is a small matter for it to supervene. The use of the hare is great for women. Dried lung, when drunk, aids the womb. For hemorrhages, the liver with Samian earth in water as a drink. The rennet for the afterbirth. They avoid daily baths. Also, application with saffron and leek juice, applied with wool, expels dead fetuses. If hare wombs are taken in food, it is thought that males will be conceived. This is also achieved by their testicles and rennet. The conception of a hare removed from the womb is said to bring lasting fertility to those who have ceased to give birth. But even the conception of a hare is healthy and is prepared by the Magi for a man. Likewise, nine grains of dung for a virgin, so that her breasts may remain firm forever. Also with the rennet. For this reason, smeared with honey, it is applied to blood where they do not wish pulled-out hairs to regrow. For swelling of the womb, wild boar or pig dung with oil is useful to apply. It stops it more effectively if flour of dry <unclear>barley</unclear> is sprinkled or if taken in a potion, such as if it torments a pregnant woman or one who has just given birth. Pig’s milk, drunk with honeyed wine, aids the delivery of women. Taken by itself, it fills the breasts of those who have just given birth if they are failing. The same, when smeared with a woman’s blood, causes the pig’s teats to grow less. If they ache, they are soothed by the drinking of ass’s milk. This, taken with added honey, also aids their purgations. The aged suet of the same animal also heals ulcerations of the womb, and applied in wool, it softens the hardness of the womb. Taken by itself, fresh or aged and applied with water, it possesses the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>depilatory agent</gloss>. The aged spleen of the same animal applied with water makes breasts abundant. It clears the face. Ass hooves, when used as a fumigant, hasten delivery, so that it may even call forth an abortion; it is not applied otherwise than to kill the living fetus. If the dung of the same animal is applied fresh, it is said to wonderfully soothe hemorrhages of blood. Also the ash of the same dung, which is also useful for the womb when applied. Horse foam, applied for forty days before the hair grows, keeps it from growing. Likewise the horn of a stag is used. It is better if the horns are fresh. The womb is aided by being washed with mare’s milk. But if one senses a dead fetus, the spleen, drunk in sweet water, expels it. Likewise, hooves as a fumigant or dry dung. It stops sagging faces if infused with butter. Bull’s gall, mixed with rose oil, opens a hardened womb, applied externally with wool and terebinth resin. They say that by fumigating with the dung of a bull, sagging wombs are pulled back, and delivery is aided. Conception, however, is aided by drinking cow’s milk. It is certain that sterility is caused by the exhaustion of childbirth. Olympias of Thebes affirms that this is corrected by bull’s gall and the fat of serpents, and verdigris with honey added to the affected areas before intercourse. Calf’s gall, if it has been sprinkled on the womb during purgations, softens the hardness of the belly and diminishes the flow, and being applied to the navel, it is useful for the whole womb. They set the measure of the gall at the weight of a denarius, mixed with a third of parsley and almond oil, as much as seems sufficient, and they apply this in wool. Male calf’s gall, ground with half the amount of honey, is applied to the womb. If they eat calf meat roasted with birthwort around the time of conception, they promise that they will give birth to males. Calf marrow, boiled in wine and water with suet, is useful for ulcerations of the womb. Likewise, fox fat, and cat excrement, applied with resin and rose oil. They consider it most useful to fumigate the womb with goat horn. The blood of wild goats with sea-palm removes hair. The gall of others, when sprinkled, softens the calluses of the womb and causes conception after purgation. Thus also the power of the depilatory agent is achieved if it is kept applied for three days after the hairs are pulled out. Midwives promise that a flow, no matter how immense, is stopped by goat urine if drunk, and if the dung is applied. The membrane of goats, kept in water and taken as a drink in wine, expels the afterbirth. They consider it useful to fumigate the womb with the hair of kids. And in a flow of blood, that the rennet be drunk or henbane seed be applied. Aeschines says that if the loins of a goat are pricked with the blood of a wild black bull, a woman will feel a weariness for sexual relations. The same says that a potion of goat urine, mixed with spikenard for the sake of fragrance, is a love charm. For infants, nothing is more useful than butter, by itself and with honey, especially in teething, and for the gums, and for ulcers of the mouth. A wolf’s tooth, tied to an infant, prevents terrors and the diseases of teething. A wolf’s skin performs the same. Indeed, their largest teeth, when tied to horses, are said to provide an indefatigable pace. A hare’s rennet, applied to the breast, stops the bowels of infants. Ass liver, with a little all-heal mixed in and dripped into the mouth, protects infants from the falling sickness and other diseases. They command this to be done for forty days. And an ass’s skin, thrown over them, makes infants fearless. The teeth that first fall out from horses provide easy teething to infants if tied to them. More effectively if they have not touched the ground. A calf’s spleen is to be eaten in honey. And it is to be applied to the pain of the spleen. For running ulcers, with honey. A calf’s spleen boiled in wine, ground, and applied, heals small ulcers of the mouth. A goat’s brain, passed through a gold ring before it is given with milk, is to be dripped into the mouths of infants against the falling sickness and other infant diseases. Goat dung, tied in a cloth, calms restless infants, especially girls. Gums smeared with goat’s milk or hare’s brain make for easy teething. Cato thinks that sleep is induced by eating hare meat. The common people also think it brings grace to the body for nine days. Yet some reason must underlie such a great belief. The Magi say that sleep is induced by the gall of a sacrificed goat applied to the eyes or placed under the pillow. The ash of goat horn in myrtle oil, when smeared on, inhibits sweating. But boar’s gall, when applied, stimulates intercourse. Likewise, the marrow of pigs when drunk. Ass suet mixed with the fat of a male goose, when applied. Likewise, the <unclear>scum</unclear> of a horse, from Virgil.

<summary>This text details various medicinal uses of animal parts (stag, wolf, hare, ass, goat, bull) to treat gynecological conditions, fertility issues, and childhood ailments.</summary>
